_note: Each moment (when + week) can have several events; the game picks one at random for each attempt (GameState.roll_events). The first one listed is the default, used by the self-test, so keep choices 0 and 1 of the first events as they are. What an event DOES depends only on the choice and the design. Before launch: add_days, add_cost_k, mult_send, mult_make, extra_mass_kg, extra_power_w, flaw (a known problem left unfixed; it can make the launch fail, see Sim.launch_risks). In orbit: add_cost_k, mult_send, mult_make, skip_week, skip_send, battery_pct, bonus_mb, fuel_pct (change), fuel_drain (extra % per week), decay_in_weeks, boost_send and boost_make (a multiplier for 'weeks' weeks). Optional per choice: protect_part (free if you fitted it), requires_part (only possible if fitted), requires_fuel (only possible with that much fuel left). Optional per event: seconds (time to decide, default 30) and timeout_choice (choice used when time runs out, default the last one). Events with a mission id only appear in that mission, and always appear there; one of their choices (the one with a real line) is what the real team did. Missing the deadline also costs a penalty (Sim.apply_timeout_penalty). hint = a free clue and advice = a clearer tip the player can pay for (event_card.gd); neither shows until asked, and no choice is highlighted. Per choice: rating (best, fair or poor) and why, shown as feedback after the choice; rating_with_part changes both when that part is fitted (Sim.choice_rating).

events.title: A part cracked on the shake table
events.body: The vibration test loosened the antenna mount. Launch shakes a spacecraft hard, which is why we test.
events.hint: Look at how close you are to the mass limit before choosing.
events.advice: If you have 0.3 kg spare, the brace is the cheapest real fix. If not, repair it: a weak mount on a heavy craft can fail at launch.

choices.label: Repair it
choices.why: Safe, but 10 days and $20k. Bracing the mount fixes it for less if you have 0.3 kg spare.
choices.detail: Costs 10 days and $20k.
choices.log: You repaired the antenna mount after the vibration test.

choices.label: Fly as it is
choices.why: A loose mount cut the radio by a quarter and raised the launch risk. Next time brace it or repair it.
choices.detail: The radio sends 25% less for the whole mission. Risky if the spacecraft is heavy (over 80% of the mass limit).
choices.log: You flew with a loose antenna mount, so the radio sent 25% less.

choices.label: Brace the mount
choices.why: The cheapest real fix: 4 days and 0.3 kg.
choices.detail: Costs 4 days and adds 0.3 kg. Watch the 4.0 kg limit.
choices.log: You strapped the antenna down with a metal brace. It added 0.3 kg.

events.title: A weak solder joint
events.body: The hot-and-cold test made a joint on the camera board crack. In orbit the temperature swings that much every 90 minutes.
events.hint: Check your spare power.
events.advice: With 3 W spare, the heater fixes it for the least time. Without the power, re-solder: flying with a cracked joint costs a fifth of your photos.

choices.label: Re-solder it
choices.why: It fixes the joint, but costs a week. A small heater stops the crack for less time, if you have 3 W spare.
choices.detail: Costs 7 days and $15k.
choices.log: You re-soldered the camera board after the thermal test.

choices.label: Fly as it is
choices.why: The cracked joint cost a fifth of your photos for the whole mission. Next time fix it before launch.
choices.detail: The camera makes 20% fewer photos for the whole mission. Risky if the spacecraft is heavy (over 80% of the mass limit).
choices.log: You flew with a weak solder joint, so the camera made 20% fewer photos.

choices.label: Add a small heater
choices.why: Keeping the board warm stops the crack, with no days lost.
choices.detail: Costs $10k and uses 3 W more power. Check your spare power.
choices.log: You added a small heater to keep the camera board warm. It uses 3 W.

events.title: A bug in the flight software
events.body: The computer froze for a few seconds during the test. You cannot send an engineer to fix it once the satellite is in orbit.
events.hint: Ask yourself: is time or money tighter on this mission?
events.advice: If your launch date has slack, the university team is free. If the date is tight, pay to fix it. Never launch software that freezes: you can't reach it in orbit.

choices.label: Fix it and retest
choices.why: Software you can't reach in orbit has to be right before launch. 5 days well spent.
choices.detail: Costs 5 days and $10k.
choices.log: You fixed the software bug and ran the test again.

choices.label: Launch with the bug
choices.why: The computer kept restarting the radio. Next time fix it: nobody can repair it in orbit.
choices.detail: The radio sends 15% less, because the computer keeps restarting it. Risky if the spacecraft is heavy (over 80% of the mass limit).
choices.log: You launched with a software bug, so the radio sent 15% less.

choices.label: Ask a university team
choices.why: Free, but 20 days is a lot of team pay. Paying to fix it was quicker.
choices.detail: Free, but they need 20 days to check the code.
choices.log: A university team checked the code for free. It took 20 days.

events.title: Solar storm
events.body: A burst of charged particles from the Sun is about to hit your satellite.
events.hint: Did you fit radiation shielding?
events.advice: With shielding, keep imaging. Without it, turning the panels away saves the photos if your battery is above about 50%; otherwise use safe mode.

choices.label: Enter safe mode
choices.why: The camera was safe, but a whole week was lost. Turning the panels away keeps the photos coming.
choices.detail: Lose this week of photos. The camera stays safe.
choices.log: You sat out the solar storm in safe mode and lost one week.

choices.label: Keep imaging
choices.why: Without shielding the storm damaged the camera. Next time fit shielding, or turn the panels away.

rating_with_part.why: Your shielding took the hit, so you lost nothing.

choices.detail: Safe only if you added radiation shielding.
choices.log_protected: Your radiation shielding protected the camera through the storm.
choices.log: The storm damaged the unshielded camera. It made half as many photos afterwards.

choices.label: Turn the panels away
choices.why: The camera stayed safe and kept working. The battery paid, not the mission.
choices.detail: Keep taking photos and protect the camera, but the battery loses 25%.
choices.log: You turned the panels away from the storm. The camera was safe, but the battery lost 25%.

events.title: Space junk ahead
events.body: A piece of old rocket is passing close to your satellite. The chance of a hit is small, but a hit would be very bad.
events.hint: A rare photo is worth something, but so is your battery.
events.advice: With the battery above about 40%, photograph it: it's free data. Without shielding, never just keep working.

choices.label: Enter safe mode
choices.why: Safe, but a week of photos lost for a small risk. A rare photo was there for the taking.
choices.detail: Lose this week of photos while the satellite hides.
choices.log: You went into safe mode while space junk passed, and lost one week.

choices.label: Keep working
choices.why: Without shielding the camera got scratched. Next time hide in safe mode, or fit shielding.

rating_with_part.why: Your shielding made it safe to keep working.

choices.detail: Safe only if you added shielding. Otherwise the camera is scratched.
choices.log_protected: Your shielding stopped the fragment. The camera was fine.
choices.log: A fragment scratched the unshielded camera. It made 40% fewer photos afterwards.

choices.label: Photograph it!
choices.why: A rare picture and extra data, for some battery.
choices.detail: A rare picture: +30 MB of data. The camera works flat out and the battery loses 15%.
choices.log: You photographed the space junk as it flew past: 30 MB of rare photos, and the battery lost 15%.

events.title: Someone else is on your channel
events.body: Another satellite is using the same radio channel. Your signal is being drowned out.
events.hint: Count how many weeks are left.
events.advice: With many weeks left, switching channel pays for itself. Near the end, waiting it out loses less data.

choices.label: Switch channel
choices.why: $15k ended the problem for the rest of the mission.
choices.detail: Costs $15k for a new radio licence. No more problem.
choices.log: You paid $15k to move to a clear radio channel.

choices.label: Put up with it
choices.why: 20% less data every week adds up. Next time switch channel: it pays for itself.
choices.detail: The radio sends 20% less for the rest of the mission.
choices.log: You stayed on the crowded channel, so the radio sent 20% less.

choices.label: Wait for it to pass
choices.why: Fine near the end of a mission. Early on, switching channel loses less.
choices.detail: The other satellite moves on in 3 weeks. Until then the radio sends 40% less.
choices.log: You waited for the other satellite to move away. The radio sent 40% less for 3 weeks.

events.title: The ground station hears nothing
events.body: A fault at the ground station means it cannot receive this week.
events.hint: Do you have storage spare and a charged battery?
events.advice: With a good battery, catching up later loses nothing and costs nothing. Rent the backup only if money is plentiful.

choices.label: Wait a week
choices.why: Nothing was lost for good, but photos piled up. Catching up later clears them.
choices.detail: No data is sent this week. Photos pile up in storage.
choices.log: You waited out the ground station fault and sent nothing for one week.

choices.label: Rent a backup station
choices.why: It works, but $30k is a lot for one week. Catching up later is free.
choices.detail: Costs $30k. Sending carries on.
choices.log_protected: Your second ground station covered the gap at no extra cost.
choices.log: You paid $30k for a backup ground station.

choices.label: Catch up later
choices.why: Nothing lost and nothing spent: the radio made up the week.
choices.detail: Send nothing now, then send 40% more for 2 weeks. The radio drains 10% of the battery.
choices.log: You saved the photos and blasted them down at 140% over the next two weeks. The battery lost 10%.

events.title: The satellite computer crashed
events.body: A cosmic ray flipped a bit in memory and the onboard computer stopped responding.
events.hint: Did you fit the fast radio?
events.advice: With the S-band radio, upload the patch: $5k and nothing is lost. Otherwise restart: losing one week beats 30% fewer photos forever.

choices.label: Restart it
choices.why: One week lost, but the computer is healthy again. A patch would have lost nothing.
choices.detail: Lose this week of photos while it reboots.
choices.log: You restarted the crashed computer and lost one week.

choices.label: Leave it running
choices.why: 30% fewer photos from then on. Next time restart it: one lost week beats a slow mission.
choices.detail: It limps along. The camera makes 30% fewer photos from now on.
choices.log: You left the glitchy computer running, so the camera made 30% fewer photos.

choices.label: Upload a patch
choices.why: A fast radio meant a cheap fix and nothing lost.
choices.detail: Costs $5k and nothing is lost. Needs a fast radio to send the patch.
choices.log: You uploaded a patch over the S-band link. The computer recovered with no downtime.

events.title: Storm over the ground station
events.body: Heavy rain is blocking the signal at your ground station.
events.hint: Rain passes; damage to photos doesn't.
events.advice: If you rented a second station it's free, so use it. Otherwise waiting costs only one week of sending.

choices.label: Wait for it to clear
choices.why: Storage fills while you wait. Smaller photos would have kept it from overflowing.
choices.detail: No data is sent this week. Photos pile up in storage.
choices.log: You waited out the storm and sent nothing for one week.

choices.label: Use a dry station abroad
choices.why: It works, but $25k for a rain shower is steep.

rating_with_part.why: Your second ground station made it free.

choices.detail: Costs $25k. Free if you added a second ground station.
choices.log_protected: Your second ground station was in the sun, so it took over for free.
choices.log: You paid $25k to use a ground station in another country.

choices.label: Take smaller photos
choices.why: Smaller files kept storage from overflowing until the rain passed.
choices.detail: Wait for the storm, but make photos a third smaller for 3 weeks so storage does not overflow.
choices.log: You waited out the storm and shrank the photos for 3 weeks so storage did not overflow.

events.title: Drifting off course
events.body: The satellite is slowly turning away from the coastlines it should photograph. Thrusters can fix it, but fuel is limited, and heavy satellites burn more of it just keeping their orbit.
events.hint: Fuel is also what keeps you in orbit later.
events.advice: Early in the mission, the small nudge keeps fuel for later trouble. Near the end, burn big: the fuel has nothing left to save.

choices.label: Big correction burn
choices.why: Perfect photos, but 30% of your fuel. You may need that fuel later.
choices.detail: Costs 30% of your fuel. The photos stay perfect.
choices.log: You burned 30% of the fuel to point the camera back at the coast.

choices.label: Small nudge
choices.why: Good enough photos and fuel saved for later trouble.
choices.detail: Costs 12% of your fuel. The camera is a little off: 15% fewer good photos.
choices.log: You used 12% of the fuel on a small nudge. The camera made 15% fewer good photos.

choices.label: Let it drift
choices.why: 30% fewer good photos for the rest of the mission. Next time use a little fuel.
choices.detail: Saves all the fuel, but the camera makes 30% fewer good photos from now on.
choices.log: You let the satellite drift to save fuel, so the camera made 30% fewer good photos.

events.title: The orbit is sinking
events.body: Thin air at this height is dragging the satellite down. If nothing is done it will burn up. Fuel is what keeps a satellite in orbit, and some may already be gone.
events.hint: How many weeks of the mission are left?
events.advice: With 40% fuel to spare, boost once and forget it. Riding it down only pays off in the last 3 weeks.

choices.label: Boost to a higher orbit
choices.why: One burn and the problem is gone for good.
choices.detail: Costs 40% of your fuel and fixes the problem for good.
choices.log: You spent 40% of the fuel to raise the orbit.

choices.label: Tiny burns every week
choices.why: It works while the fuel lasts, but it drains you every week.
choices.detail: Costs 2% more fuel every week. You keep your orbit as long as the fuel lasts.
choices.log: You switched to tiny burns every week, which cost 2% more fuel each week.

choices.label: Ride it down
choices.why: Sharper photos, but the satellite burned up. Next time boost to a higher orbit.
choices.detail: A lower orbit takes sharper photos (25% more), but the satellite burns up in 3 weeks.
choices.log: You let the orbit sink for sharper photos. The satellite would burn up in 3 weeks.

events.title: No room for a data recorder?
events.body: The radiation counter works, but nothing on board can store readings between ground stations. A small recorder takes time and mass.
events.hint: Where is the satellite most of the time: over a station, or not?
events.advice: Ground stations only see the satellite for a few minutes each orbit. Without storage, most readings are never heard.

choices.label: Fly without a recorder
choices.detail: No delay, but the radio sends 40% less.
choices.why: Most readings were lost between stations. Next time, make room to store data.
choices.log: You chose: Fly without a recorder.
choices.real: This is what the Explorer 1 team did in 1958: readings were only caught over ground stations. Explorer 3 flew a tape recorder two months later.

choices.label: Add a small recorder
choices.detail: 6 days and 0.2 kg.
choices.why: Readings are stored and sent when a station is in view.
choices.log: You chose: Add a small recorder.

choices.label: Rent more ground stations
choices.why: More passes help, but storage would catch everything for less.
choices.log: You chose: Rent more ground stations.

events.title: The first full test, live on TV
events.body: This is the first launch of the complete rocket, and the whole country is watching. The engineers want more ground tests of the first stage first.
events.hint: How many times has this exact rocket flown?
events.advice: A rocket's first full flight is a test. Test more on the ground, or fly it without the precious payload.

choices.label: Launch on schedule
choices.detail: No delay. Two untested parts fly.
choices.why: The untested stage failed at lift-off. Next time, test more on the ground first.
choices.log: You chose: Launch on schedule.
choices.real: This is what happened with Vanguard TV-3 in 1957: under huge pressure after Sputnik, the first full Vanguard launched on live TV, rose about a metre and exploded.

choices.label: Run more ground tests
choices.detail: 10 days and $15k.
choices.why: Problems found on the ground cost days, not the rocket.
choices.log: You chose: Run more ground tests.

choices.label: Fly a test without the satellite
choices.detail: 20 days.
choices.why: Safe, but slow. More ground tests would have found the same faults sooner.
choices.log: You chose: Fly a test without the satellite.

events.title: The path keeps drifting
events.body: Every small thruster firing pushes the spacecraft a little off the predicted path. The team keeps correcting it by hand.
events.hint: If a number keeps coming out wrong, is the problem the flight, or the number?
events.advice: A drift that never goes away usually means one input is wrong. Trace the thruster data back to where it comes from, units included.

choices.label: Keep correcting by hand
choices.detail: Nothing changes for now.
choices.why: The cause was never found, and the spacecraft flew too low. Next time, trace the error to its source.
choices.log: You chose: Keep correcting by hand.
choices.real: This is what happened to Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999: one team's software gave thruster data in pound-force seconds, another expected newton-seconds. The drift was noticed but never traced, and the orbiter was lost in Mars' atmosphere.

choices.label: Check every number, units too
choices.detail: Lose this week while you check.
choices.why: The units mismatch was found and fixed. A week lost, a mission saved.
choices.log: You chose: Check every number, units too.

choices.label: Do an extra correction burn
choices.detail: 15% of the fuel.
choices.why: It buys time, but the wrong number is still there.
choices.log: You chose: Do an extra correction burn.

events.title: Not much heat margin
events.body: The thermal model says the probe will stay cool enough in a 100 km orbit, but with little to spare. Heat from the Moon's surface is hard to predict.
events.hint: What happens if the model is a little wrong?
events.advice: Leave margin where you are least sure. A bigger radiator costs a little mass now and saves the mission later.

choices.label: Trust the model and fly
choices.detail: No delay. The camera makes 20% less once it overheats.
choices.why: It ran hot in orbit. Next time, leave heat margin where the model is least sure.
choices.log: You chose: Trust the model and fly.
choices.real: Chandrayaan-1 (2008) ran hotter than expected in lunar orbit. ISRO raised its orbit from 100 to 200 km to cool it down, and contact was lost after 312 days.

choices.label: Add a bigger radiator
choices.detail: 5 days and 0.3 kg.
choices.why: With margin, the probe stays cool all mission.
choices.log: You chose: Add a bigger radiator.

choices.label: Plan a higher, cooler orbit
choices.detail: Photos are a little less sharp (10% less).
choices.why: It works, but a radiator would keep the sharper orbit.
choices.log: You chose: Plan a higher, cooler orbit.

events.title: Another close-approach warning
events.body: The tracking list says a dead satellite will pass near yours. Warnings like this come every week, and most are false alarms.
events.hint: How bad is it if this one is not a false alarm?
events.advice: A small dodge costs a little fuel. A collision costs everything. When it is cheap to move, move.

choices.label: Ignore it
choices.detail: Nothing changes, probably.
choices.why: This time it was real. Next time, a small dodge is cheap insurance.
choices.log: You chose: Ignore it.
choices.real: Iridium 33 did not move in February 2009: warnings were common. The dead Kosmos-2251 hit it at about 11.7 km per second.

choices.label: Do a small dodge burn
choices.detail: 8% of the fuel.
choices.why: A little fuel, and the junk passed safely.
choices.log: You chose: Do a small dodge burn.

choices.label: Ask for a better tracking estimate
choices.why: Better data helps, but a dodge would have been cheaper and safer.
choices.log: You chose: Ask for a better tracking estimate.

events.title: The window to Mars is closing
events.body: Earth and Mars line up for a launch only every 26 months. The flight software has not finished testing.
events.hint: Can the software be fixed after launch?
events.advice: Never launch untested software you depend on to leave Earth. Test the critical commands now, even if it costs days.

choices.label: Launch now, fix it in flight
choices.detail: No delay. Two untested parts fly.
choices.why: The software failed and the probe was stuck. Next time, test the critical commands before launch.

effects.label: no test of the engine-start commands

choices.log: You chose: Launch now, fix it in flight.
choices.real: This is what happened to Fobos-Grunt in 2011: it launched with its software not fully tested, its engines never fired to leave Earth orbit, and it fell back two months later.

choices.label: Test the critical commands
choices.detail: 10 days.
choices.why: The engine-start commands are proven before launch.
choices.log: You chose: Test the critical commands.

choices.label: Wait for the next window
choices.detail: 40 days in the game (26 months in real life).
choices.why: Safe, but very slow. Testing the critical parts now was enough.
choices.log: You chose: Wait for the next window.

events.title: New thruster settings
events.body: After a software update, the team has new thruster settings to upload. They have not been run on the simulator yet.
events.hint: What could a wrong thruster setting do to a spinning spacecraft?
events.advice: Run every new setting on the simulator first. Thrusters fire on their own, and a wrong one can make things worse.

choices.label: Upload them now
choices.detail: No delay.
choices.why: The wrong setting made it spin faster until parts broke off. Next time, test it on the simulator first.
choices.log: You chose: Upload them now.
choices.real: This is what happened to Hitomi in 2016: after an attitude error, a wrong thruster setting that had not been checked made the telescope spin faster until parts broke off.

choices.label: Test them on the simulator
choices.why: The simulator caught the wrong setting before it flew.
choices.log: You chose: Test them on the simulator.

choices.label: Keep the old settings
choices.detail: The camera points less well: 15% fewer photos.
choices.why: Safe, but testing the new settings would have been better.
choices.log: You chose: Keep the old settings.

events.title: A storm is forecast
events.body: Space weather forecasters expect a geomagnetic storm just after launch. A storm heats the upper air and makes it thicker, which drags low satellites down.
events.hint: How high will your satellite be released?
events.advice: Satellites released very low are the most at risk from drag. Wait a few days, or release higher.

choices.label: Launch, release low as planned
choices.detail: No delay. The satellite has 3 weeks before drag pulls it down.
choices.why: The storm dragged it down. Next time, wait for the storm to pass.
choices.log: You chose: Launch, release low as planned.
choices.real: This is what happened to Starlink Group 4-7 in February 2022: the satellites were released low (about 210 km) as a storm arrived, and about 38 of 49 burned up.

choices.label: Wait a few days
choices.detail: 5 days.
choices.why: The storm passed and the satellite climbed safely.
choices.log: You chose: Wait a few days.

choices.label: Launch, but release higher
choices.detail: $30k for the extra rocket performance.
choices.why: It works, but waiting a few days was cheaper.
choices.log: You chose: Launch, but release higher.

events.title: Which rocket?
events.body: A new low-cost small rocket can launch your CubeSats for much less, but it has only flown a few times.
events.hint: What happens to all of them if that one rocket fails?
events.advice: Never put everything on one unproven rocket. Spread the risk, or pay for a proven one.

choices.label: All of them on the new rocket
choices.detail: Cheap. Two risks fly together.
choices.why: One failure took everything. Next time, spread the risk.
choices.log: You chose: All of them on the new rocket.

choices.label: New rocket, but split over launches
choices.detail: 10 days. One risk.
choices.why: Spreading the satellites limited the loss.
choices.log: You chose: New rocket, but split over launches.
choices.real: This is what NASA did for TROPICS: three launches planned on Astra's Rocket 3.3. The first, in June 2022, failed and two CubeSats were lost; the other four flew on Rocket Lab's Electron in 2023 and worked.

choices.label: Pay for a proven rocket
choices.why: More money, much less risk.
choices.log: You chose: Pay for a proven rocket.
